newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Rebels enter Zaire's 2nd city, Mobutu names new PM.
newsitem.headline: Rebels enter Zaire's 2nd city, Mobutu names new PM.

text.p: Laurent Kabila's rebels entered Zaire's second city of Lubumbashi on Wednesday with residents hailing them as liberators and pressure increased on President Mobutu Sese Seko to stand down.

While Washington suggested the time had come for the veteran leader to go, Mobutu named a senior general as emergency rule prime minister in the capital Kinshasa where his army clashed with thousands of supporters of arch-foe Etienne Tshisekedi.
Tshisekedi, a veteran opposition leader and prime minister for less than a week, tried in vain on Wednesday to make his way to the prime minister's office complex to install his new team.

Witnesses said Mobutu's son Kongolo and other soldiers, who barred the route with armoured vehicles, escorted Tshisekedi back to his home in Kinshasa's Limete district. Tshisekedi was bleeding from a slight head wound.

The rebels, who now control almost half of the sprawling Central African nation, entered Lubumbashi after meeting stiff resistance from Mobutu loyalists on the approaches to the Shaba province capital of one million people.

"We are too happy, too happy. We were colonised for 35 years by that dictator Mobutu. He looted our Katanga (Shaba)," said Henri Kisimuzima, 48, security chief at the city's main hotel, the Karavia, after rebels arrived there.
Critics accuse Mobutu and his cronies of amassing fortunes while most of Zaire's 45 million people live in abject poverty in what is potentially one of Africa's richest countries.

Rebels pressed on towards Lubumbashi city centre. Residents said Zairean soldiers were nowhere to be seen and there had been no sign of looting that traditionally accompanies the withdrawal of Zaire's ill-disciplined army.
Mobutu has dominated Zaire since seizing power in 1965 but his hold over the nation has crumbled as the rebels have advanced. He decreed a nationwide state of emergency on Tuesday.

Witnesses said security forces fired in the air in Kinshasa and used teargas to break up crowds of thousands of supporters of Tshisekedi, whose power base is in the teeming slums of the capital of over five million people.
"The new state of emergency is for the dustbin. Mobutu made the decision all alone," Tshisekedi's minister of posts and telecommunications, Modeste Kikunga, told Reuters.
"We won't take this lying down. They will find us in their path," one Tshisekedi aide said on hearing that Mobutu had appointed General Likulia Bolongo prime minister in place of Tshisekedi.
Likulia was defence minister in the pre-Tshisekedi administration of Kengo wa Dondo. The transitional parliament voted out Kengo following persistent charges that he mismanaged the war in the east.
The television said Mobutu named Likulia because Zaire's political family had withdrawn its support for Tshisekedi.

Tshisekedi fell foul of Mobutu supporters and allies alike after announcing a government composed only of his most loyal followers. He earmaked six posts for rebels, who took up arms in October vowing to topple Mobutu, but the offer was rebuffed.
In Washington, White House spokesman Mike McCurry said that Mobutuism, which flourished with U.S. support during the Cold War, "is about to become a creature of history".
He said Mobutu should stand down and transitional arrangements made. "The support for President Mobutu is not sufficient to lead Zaire into the next chapter of its history," he told reporters.
